docs.title: Shalom - Declarative GraphQL Client for Flutter & Dart
docs.text:
Declarative GraphQL for Flutter & Dart

Backed by a high-performance Rust runtime with normalized caching, optimistic updates, and reactive entity-level subscriptions.

Get Started → View Quickstart ⚡ Rust-Powered Core

A full-fledged GraphQL runtime written in Rust handles normalized caching, link execution, GC, and optimistic mutations with zero UI-thread overhead.

🪄 Declarative Codegen

Annotate your Flutter widgets with @Query, @Mutation, and @Fragment. No manual glue, no separate .graphql operation files.

🎯 Reactive Scopes

Generated fragment Ref and Scope types keep individual list items and widgets in sync without global state management solutions.

docs.title: Custom Scalars
docs.text: Shalom lets you map GraphQL custom scalars to Dart types with a small config file and a CustomScalarImpl implementation. The generated code will use your Dart type for fields and call the serializer/deserializer automatically.

docs.title: 1. Define a Dart type and scalar implementation
docs.text:
import 'package:shalom/shalom.dart';

class Point {
  final int x;
  final int y;

  const Point({required this.x, required this.y});

  @override
  String toString() => 'Point(x: $x, y: $y)';

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) =>
      identical(this, other) || (other is Point && other.x == x && other.y == y);

  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hash(x, y);
}

class _PointScalarImpl implements CustomScalarImpl<Point> {
  @override
  Point deserialize(dynamic raw) {
    if (raw is Map<String, dynamic>) {
      if (!raw.containsKey('x')) {
        throw FormatException("Point expects field 'x' but it was missing.");
      }
      if (!raw.containsKey('y')) {
        throw FormatException("Point expects field 'y' but it was missing.");
      }
      if (raw['x'] is! int || raw['y'] is! int) {
        throw FormatException("Point expects integer fields 'x' and 'y'.");
      }
      return Point(x: raw['x'], y: raw['y']);
    }

    if (raw is! String) {
      throw FormatException("Expected String or Map for Point, got ${raw.runtimeType}.");
    }

    final regex = RegExp(r'POINT\s*\((-?\d+),\s*(-?\d+)\)');
    final match = regex.firstMatch(raw);
    if (match == null) throw FormatException("Invalid POINT format: $raw");

    return Point(x: int.parse(match[1]!), y: int.parse(match[2]!));
  }

  @override
  dynamic serialize(Point value) => "POINT (${value.x}, ${value.y})";
}

final pointScalarImpl = _PointScalarImpl();

docs.title: 2. Register the scalar in shalom.yml
docs.text:
Create a shalom.yml in your project root:

custom_scalars:
  Point:
    graphql_name: "Point"
    output_type:
      import_path: "package:my_app/point.dart"
      symbol_name: "Point"
    impl_symbol:
      import_path: "package:my_app/point.dart"
      symbol_name: "pointScalarImpl"

Field types will be generated as Point, and requests will use pointScalarImpl for serialization and deserialization.

docs.title: 3. Use the scalar in your schema
docs.text:
scalar Point

type Location {
  id: ID!
  coordinates: Point!
}

Run shalom generate --path . again to update your Dart types.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Shalom ships a Rust-based CLI for code generation and Dart packages for runtime support. This guide covers the minimal setup for a Flutter app using Shalom's declarative annotation API.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Rust toolchain (for the CLI)
  • Flutter SDK (Shalom's declarative widgets are Flutter-only)

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
cargo install --git https://github.com/nrbnlulu/shalom.git --branch main shalom_dart_codegen

The command installs the shalom binary on your PATH.

docs.title: Add Dart dependencies
docs.text:
dependencies:
  shalom: ^0.1.5
  shalom_flutter: ^0.1.5
  shalom_annotations: ^0.1.5

Or add them via the Flutter CLI:

flutter pub add shalom shalom_flutter shalom_annotations
  • package:shalom exposes ShalomRuntimeClient, links (HttpLink, WebSocketLink), response types, and cache helpers.
  • package:shalom_flutter exposes ShalomProvider/ShalomScope, generated widget base classes, fragment scopes, and the debug panel.
  • package:shalom_annotations provides @Query, @Mutation, @Subscription, and @Fragment, which the codegen scans for.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
The codegen scans your Dart/Flutter source tree for classes annotated with @Query / @Mutation / @Subscription / @Fragment. You still need a GraphQL schema file schema.graphql for validation and type generation. A common layout is:

my_flutter_app/
├── lib/
│   ├── graphql/
│   │   └── schema.graphql      # GraphQL schema
│   ├── albums_page.dart        # @Query widget
│   ├── album_widget.dart       # @Fragment widget
│   └── __graphql__/            # Generated code (auto-created)
├── shalom.yml                  # Optional config (custom scalars, etc.)
└── pubspec.yaml

Generated files are written next to their source files under a __graphql__ directory (for example lib/__graphql__/albums_page.widget.shalom.dart). Do not edit files under __graphql__ directly.

optional shalom.yml

The shalom.yml configuration is optional unless you need custom scalars mappings or custom output options.

docs.title: CLI usage
docs.text:
Generate code once:

shalom generate --path .

Watch for changes and re-generate on save:

shalom watch --path .

Both commands scan .graphql schema files and annotated .dart files under the given path (skipping generated __graphql__ directories).

docs.title: Normalized Cache
docs.text: Shalom's Rust runtime stores GraphQL responses in a normalized cache so the same entity can be updated across multiple queries, subscriptions, mutations, and fragments. Instead of embedding nested objects directly, it keys root operation results (ROOT_QUERY, ROOT_MUTATION, ROOT_SUBSCRIPTION) and entity records such as Album:123 by identity, and stores references from parent objects down to them.

docs.title: What this means in practice
docs.text:
• An Album fetched by a query and read again by a fragment widget is stored once in the cache.
  • When any response includes the same entity, the cache entry is updated and every active observer of that entity re-emits the latest data.
  • Generated @Query / @Subscription / @Fragment widgets register as cache observers automatically (marked with the @observe directive in generated SDL) — you don't call subscribe/observe yourself in normal usage.
  • List membership (adding/removing/reordering items) is not inferred from a mutation response alone. If a mutation creates, deletes, or reorders items and the response doesn't include the parent list field, update the cached query or fragment yourself with executeWithCacheUpdate (see below).

docs.title: Example flow
docs.text:
1. AlbumsPage, a @Query widget, fetches albums { ...AlbumWidget } and normalizes each album into the cache under Album:<id>.
  2. AlbumWidget, a @Fragment widget, is mounted for each album via its generated ref (AlbumWidgetRef.fromId(id)), and observes that same Album:<id> entity.
  3. A mutation that returns fields on that Album (for example renaming it) updates the shared cache entry, so both AlbumsPage's list item and any standalone AlbumWidgetScope showing that album re-ruender immediately.
// Mounting a fragment reactively via its Scope:
AlbumWidgetScope(
  ref: AlbumWidgetRef.fromId(albumId),
  builder: (context, album) => Text(album.name),
)

docs.title: When to rely on it
docs.text: Use the normalized cache implicitly by default: mount generated @Query / @Subscription widgets for screen-level data, and @Fragment widgets/XScope for reactive, entity-scoped UI. Because reads are cache-first by default (ExecutionPolicyInput.cacheFirst), the UI re-renders whenever normalized data changes, even if that change came from a different operation or a mutation elsewhere in the app.

docs.title: Updating lists after mutations
docs.text:
When a mutation creates, deletes, adds, or removes items, the mutation response normalizes the target entity automatically, but GraphQL servers typically don't return the entire parent list.

Use executeWithCacheUpdate to read the cached query or fragment, modify the list, and write it back:

docs.title: 1. Adding an item to a root query list
docs.text:
await CreateAlbumMutation(client).executeWithCacheUpdate(
  name: name,
  update: (cache, data) async {
    final current = await AlbumsPageData.readFrom(cache);
    if (current == null) return;

    final newRef = AlbumWidgetRef.fromId(data.createAlbum.id);
    await cache.writeOperation(
      data: AlbumsPageData(
        albums: [...current.albums, newRef],
      ),
    );
  },
);

docs.title: 2. Updating or removing items from a nested entity list
docs.text:
await RemoveGifFromAlbumMutation(client).executeWithCacheUpdate(
  albumId: albumId,
  gifId: gifId,
  update: (cache, data) async {
    if (data.removeGifFromAlbum != null) return;

    final current = await AlbumWidgetRef.fromId(albumId).readFrom(cache);
    if (current == null) return;

    await cache.writeFragment(
      data: AlbumWidgetData(
        id: current.id,
        name: current.name,
        tag: current.tag,
        gifs: current.gifs.where((g) => g.id != gifId).toList(),
      ),
    );
  },
);

docs.title: Invalidating operations
docs.text: When patching the cache by hand isn't practical (e.g. server-side sorting, pagination, or computed fields), invalidate the affected operations instead. Invalidation evicts the operation's root cache entry and signals its matching active subscriptions to refetch fresh data from the network on their existing streams.

docs.title: After a mutation
docs.text:
Every generated mutation execute (as well as executeWithCacheUpdate and executeOptimistic) accepts invalidateOperations. They only run once the mutation succeeds:

await AddPostMutation(client).execute(
  input: AddPostInput(title: 'Hello'),
  invalidateOperations: [
    // Every active instance of GetPosts, regardless of variables:
    OperationRef(operationName: $GetPostsQuery.operation$Name()),
    // Only the instance matching these variables:
    OperationRef(
      operationName: $GetPostQuery.operation$Name(),
      variables: GetPostQueryVariables(id: '123').toShalomValue(),
    ),
  ],
);

docs.title: Optimistic updates
docs.text:
Use generated executeOptimistic when you want instant UI feedback before the network responds:

final result = await RenameAlbumMutation(client).executeOptimistic(
  (vars) => RenameAlbumMutationData(
    renameAlbum: RenameAlbumMutation_renameAlbum(
      id: vars.id,
      name: vars.name,
    ),
  ),
  id: albumId,
  name: nextName,
  rollbackWhen: (data) => data.renameAlbum == null,
);
  • Normalizes the predicted payload immediately and notifies any widget or fragment observing that entity record.
  • Automatically rolls back if the network call throws or if rollbackWhen evaluates to true.
  • Returns an OptimisticMutationResponse with response and an async rollback() method.

docs.title: Garbage collection
docs.text:
The runtime only keeps a root operation field (and entities reachable through it) alive while some active subscription still references it.

One-shot imperative reads

A one-shot imperative read (client.request(...).first) never registers as an active subscriber, so its data becomes eligible for eviction the moment any other cache activity triggers GC. For a one-off read that should stay live for as long as the UI cares about it, mount the generated @Query widget conditionally instead of using a one-shot imperative request.

docs.title: Debugging the cache
docs.text:
package:shalom_flutter includes a ShalomDebugPanel widget that renders the live normalized cache next to your app, useful for verifying that entities normalize and update the way you expect:

ShalomDebugPanel(client: ShalomScope.of(context))

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Shalom is a declarative GraphQL client for Dart and Flutter, backed by a Rust runtime (normalized cache, links, execution, cache subscriptions).

docs.title: Paradigm
docs.text:
Shalom is declarative: as a rule of thumb you don't need services or state management solutions for GraphQL data. You annotate widget classes with @Query, @Mutation, @Subscription, or @Fragment, and the codegen wires them to a normalized cache that keeps every widget observing it in sync.

  • Every widget should request only what it needs.
  • Prefer server-side work (sorting, filtering, pagination) over UI-side work, since list items are usually fragments and aren't declaratively readable by a list builder.
  • Reads are declarative (generated widgets/scopes); mutations are imperative (generated mutation classes called from event handlers).

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Rust runtime with a normalized cache, so the same entity read by different operations stays in sync everywhere it's rendered.
  • Annotation-driven codegen: @Query / @Mutation / @Subscription / @Fragment on plain Dart/Flutter classes, no separate .graphql operation files.
  • Generated fragment Ref/Scope types for reactive, entity-scoped widgets.
  • Cache-aware mutation helpers: execute, executeWithCacheUpdate, executeOptimistic.
  • Custom scalar support via a small Dart glue layer.
  • A Flutter debug panel for inspecting the live normalized cache.

To get started, check out the Installation guide and the Quickstart walkthrough. You can also explore examples/flutter/gif_search in the repository for a complete working app.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This walkthrough is a hands-on tutorial for the GIF search Flutter example in examples/flutter/gif_search. The same approach works for any Flutter app using Shalom's declarative annotation API.

docs.title: 1. Add your schema
docs.text:
Shalom still needs a GraphQL schema for validation and type generation. The example keeps it at examples/flutter/gif_search/lib/graphql/schema.graphql:

type Album {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  tag: String!
  gifs: [Gif!]!
}

type Gif {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  url: String!
}

docs.title: 2. Annotate widgets, fragments, and mutations
docs.text:
There are no separate .graphql operation files. You annotate the Dart/Flutter classes that need data directly, and the codegen generates a $ClassName base class alongside them:

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:shalom_annotations/shalom_annotations.dart';
import 'package:gif_search/__graphql__/AlbumsPage.widget.shalom.dart';
import 'package:gif_search/__graphql__/AlbumWidget.shalom.dart';

@Query(r"""
  {
    albums {
      ...AlbumWidget
    }
  }
""")
class AlbumsPage extends $AlbumsPage {
  const AlbumsPage({super.key});

  @override
  Widget buildData(BuildContext context, AlbumsPageData data) {
    return ListView.builder(
      itemCount: data.albums.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, i) => AlbumWidget(ref: data.albums[i]),
    );
  }
}

@Fragment(r"""
  on Album {
    id
    name
    tag
    gifs { id title url }
  }
""")
class AlbumWidget extends $AlbumWidget {
  const AlbumWidget({super.key, required super.ref});

  @override
  Widget buildData(BuildContext context, AlbumWidgetData album) =>
      ListTile(title: Text(album.name));
}

You can also annotate mutation classes to generate type-safe mutation executors:

import 'package:gif_search/__graphql__/CreateAlbumMutation.mutation.shalom.dart';

@Mutation(r"""
  ($name: String!) {
    createAlbum(name: $name) {
      id
      name
      tag
    }
  }
""")
class CreateAlbumMutation extends $CreateAlbumMutation {
  const CreateAlbumMutation(super.client);
}

Mutations are executed imperatively with generated executor classes:

final client = ShalomScope.of(context);
final response = await CreateAlbumMutation(client).execute(name: 'Favorites');

docs.title: 3. Run codegen
docs.text:
shalom generate --path examples/flutter/gif_search

Shalom emits Dart files under a __graphql__ directory next to each annotated file (for example lib/__graphql__/AlbumsPage.widget.shalom.dart and lib/__graphql__/AlbumWidget.shalom.dart). It also emits a single registration file next to your schema under lib/graphql/__graphql__/shalom_init.shalom.dart, exporting kSchemaSdl, registerShalomDefinitions(client), and the app-scoped ShalomProvider.

docs.title: 4. Create the client and register definitions
docs.text:
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:shalom/shalom.dart';
import 'package:gif_search/graphql/__graphql__/shalom_init.shalom.dart'
    show kSchemaSdl, registerShalomDefinitions, ShalomProvider;

void main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await ShalomRuntimeClient.initFlutterRustBridge();

  final client = ShalomRuntimeClient.create(
    schemaSdl: kSchemaSdl,
    link: HttpLink(transportLayer: transport, url: graphqlUrl),
  );
  registerShalomDefinitions(client);

  runApp(ShalomProvider(client: client, child: const MyApp()));
}

ShalomProvider puts the client above your widget tree so generated query/subscription/fragment widgets and ShalomScope.of(context) can find it.

docs.title: 5. Mount the generated widget
docs.text:
There is no manual request/subscribe call for reads. Just place the annotated widget in the tree:

home: const AlbumsPage(),

AlbumsPage fetches on mount, normalizes the response into the cache, and rebuilds whenever a watched cache entry changes — including changes written by other operations or mutations.

docs.title: 6. Handle loading, error, and data states
docs.text:
For @Query and @Subscription widgets, buildLoading, buildError, and buildData are all abstract methods that must be implemented:

  • buildLoading(BuildContext context): Displayed while the query or subscription is in flight and no cached data is available.
  • buildError(BuildContext context, Object error): Displayed when a request fails with an error and no cached fallback exists.
  • buildData(BuildContext context, T data): Called whenever data is ready or updated from the normalized cache.

For @Fragment widgets, buildLoading (defaults to SizedBox.shrink()) and buildError (defaults to ErrorWidget) have default implementations, while buildData is required. You can override them as needed:

@override
Widget buildLoading(BuildContext context) =>
    const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());

@override
Widget buildError(BuildContext context, Object error) =>
    Center(child: Text('Error: $error'));

Reusing loading and error states

In real applications, you can define a mixin (like QueryWidgetMixin) to avoid repeating buildLoading and buildError implementations across your screens:

mixin QueryWidgetMixin {
  Widget buildLoading(BuildContext context) =>
      const Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator());

  Widget buildError(BuildContext context, Object error) =>
      Center(child: Text('Error: $error'));
}

class MyQueryScreen extends $MyQueryScreen with QueryWidgetMixin {
  @override
  Widget buildData(BuildContext context, MyQueryData data) => ...;
}

docs.title: 7. (Optional) Configure shalom.yml
docs.text:
A shalom.yml configuration file in your project root is optional, but lets you configure custom scalar mappings or override output directories:

custom_scalars: {}

See the Custom Scalars guide for details on mapping custom GraphQL types to Dart classes.

docs.title: 8. Run the example app
docs.text:
The example app includes a local mock GraphQL server in examples/flutter/gif_search/server.

Start the mock server (in one terminal):

cd examples/flutter/gif_search/server
uv run python main.py

The server runs on http://127.0.0.1:7000/graphql and includes a GraphiQL playground.

Then, start the Flutter app (in another terminal):

cd examples/flutter/gif_search
flutter run

docs.title: 9. Next: Normalized Cache
docs.text:
Shalom normalizes response data into typed entity records (e.g. Album:<id>), so a change from one operation (a mutation, another query, or a subscription) immediately updates every widget that reads the same entity — with zero prop drilling or manual refetching.

Head over to the Normalized Cache guide!
